abstract: Marine heatwaves are restructuring coral reefs, but monitoring coral community change across impacted habitats and reefs remains expensive and logistically challenging. Metabarcoding of seawater DNA represents a potential solution to the issue of scale, but technical challenges and a lack of ground truthing with conventional measures of coral community structure have limited its application. In early 2025, Mermaid Reef in the Rowley Shoals, a remote oceanic atoll in northwest Australia, experienced unprecedented heat stress resulting in widespread coral bleaching and mortality. Using photo-transect data alongside seawater eDNA samples, we quantified changes in coral cover and community assemblage before and after the heatwave and compared results of the two monitoring methods. Photo-transect data showed sharp reductions in live coral cover, particularly in Acropora, the dominant pre-bleaching genus. eDNA data mirrored these shifts, and Acropora sequences dominated pre-bleaching samples but declined strongly after bleaching, while several less abundant genera increased in relative read abundance. Across sites and timepoints, eDNA reads corresponded to photo-transect cover, and multivariate assemblage patterns strongly aligned between the two methods. These results demonstrate that seawater eDNA metabarcoding can provide rapid detection of community restructuring on coral reefs and can augment existing monitoring frameworks.
